## Introduction

<!-- Problem background and overview of the approach. -->

Handwriting styles vary between individuals and develop over years of practice, making handwriting a distinctive yet subtle biometric trait. Writer identification from handwritten samples has practical applications in forensic document examination, authorship attribution, and biometric authentication [@Abushahla2026]. Advances in machine learning enable models to learn discriminative features directly from raw images, providing an opportunity to investigate how effectively different architectures capture writer-specific characteristics.

This report uses a dataset of 25,000 images of handwritten digits (0-4), contributed by 20 writers over 5 sessions, with 50 samples per digit, writer and session. The dataset enables investigation of within-session and between-session variation, while its limited number of writers and structured sampling inform the experimental design and evaluation strategy.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are a class of neural networks designed to hierarchically learn spatial features from image data [@Reza2026; @Yamashita2018]. Convolutional layers apply filters to learn local patterns such as stroke edges and curves; pooling layers summarise these features into lower-dimensional representations, retaining the most important information while reducing sensitivity to small positional changes. The extracted features are subsequently passed to fully connected layers, which produce predictions over the possible writer classes, with the final layer outputting a probability distribution across the classes. In this application, the CNN is trained to answer: which writer produced this image?

Siamese neural networks (SNNs) reframe this question. Rather than assigning an image to a writer, a SNN takes two images and asks: were these written by the same person? Both images are processed by identical CNN subnetworks with shared weights, producing embeddings that represent learned visual characteristics. The distance between the embeddings provides a measure of the similarity between the two samples. The network is trained to encourage same-writer images to have embeddings close together and push different-writer embeddings further apart, using a contrastive loss function. A threshold on the embedding distance then converts it into a binary classification of same or different [@He2025]. 

Introduced originally for signature verification [@Bromley1993] and subsequently applied to other recognition tasks, SNNs have demonstrated potential across a range of applications, including signature identification [@herman_2026] and malware image classification [@Hsiao_2019]. Their ability to learn pairwise similarities makes them well-suited to handwriting verification. Moreover, their effectiveness in one-shot learning has been demonstrated in malware image classification, where similarity-based learning enables classification with limited training data [@Hsiao_2019]. In the context of handwriting verification, evaluating performance on writers excluded from training provides a means of assessing the model's ability to generalise to unseen writers.

This report compares CNN-based writer identification and SNN-based writer verification to investigate how effectively each approach distinguishes individual writing styles in handwritten digit images. It explores the dataset, evaluates both architectures, and compares their performance across hyperparameter configurations, writing sessions, and digit classes, highlighting their respective strengths and limitations.

The analysis was conducted in R version 4.6.1 [@R]. Both CNNs and Siamese networks were fitted using the Keras framework via the *keras3* R package [@keras3] using the TensorFlow backend [@tensorflow]. The tidyverse package [@tidyverse] was utilised throughout the analysis for data manipulation and plotting using *ggplot2.*
